interactions.summary: A student reasons that the friend now sees the marriage as a bad alliance that destroys power rather than securing it, and Jiang pushes the point by asking how the friend would look if he became associated with a mother-slaying coercer.

A student asks whether the friend has a moral obligation to refuse the marriage, and Jiang answers by expanding the case into a general lesson: life is irreducibly complex, each person follows a vow under uncertainty, and divine intervention can reorder events in ways strategy cannot predict.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student moral question with Jiang answer

interactions.summary: Jiang ends the sequence by inviting another question, signaling that the thought experiment has served its teaching purpose.

claims.claim: The student argues that once the friend sees the coercion, the marriage no longer produces power or alliance but instead destroys the very family and political order it was meant to secure.
Jiang reinforces that the friend would inherit moral and reputational contamination by aligning himself with a man willing to threaten his own mother.
Jiang says the real lesson is that nothing in life is as simple as it seems and that hard choices cannot be solved by flat moral formulas.
Jiang frames Dante's answer to such dilemmas as faith-led intuition: each actor cannot fully map consequences, so faith in God is what leads toward the right choice.
Jiang argues that the thought experiment shows strategy is radically limited: God can intervene through other people and reorder outcomes in ways no one can fully plan.

claims.claim: Jiang concludes that intuition, faith, and will are the best guides because events will manifest beyond what deliberate strategizing can foresee.
claims.temporal_scope: Conclusion to the thought experiment on 2026-06-16.
